newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-New look CVRD to turn multinational.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-New look CVRD to turn multinational.

text.p: Critics say he is too young and inexperienced to run the world's largest iron ore exporter, but 43-year-old entrepreneur Benjamin Steinbruch promises he will turn Brazil's privatized mining giant CVRD into a multinational force.
The international Valepar consortium led by Steinbruch won Latin America's largest privatization to date by bidding $3.15 billion for a controling stake in the mining conglomerate May 6.

"Our proposal is to turn CVRD into a multinational under Brazilian flag, one that we can all be proud of," CVRD's new chairman told Reuters during a recent interview. "CVRD, today, is in a position to understand what is being done out there and to do exactly the same."

A number of Brazilian press articles have questioned whether Steinbruch, who started out his own business career in the textile industry as member of his family's Vicunha empire, has the experience to run a mining giant.
Steinbruch told Reuters he does not see the lack of mining experience of Valepar's members as a stumbling block to future success.

"It's better that way because you can contract services or look for partners that you judge to be the best in a particular area, rather than being obliged to work with an existing partner who is not necessarily the best in the market," he said.

Apart from Brazilian steelmaker CSN of which Steinbruch is chairman, Valepar's members are local pension funds, NationsBank Corp, Opportunity Asset Management's offshore investment fund, CVRD employees and the investment arm of Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDESpar).
Steinbruch and his partners are still feeling their way around CVRD's far flung operations which reach from remote areas in the Amazon to the southeastern state of Minas Gerais.

They have given themselves six months to study CVRD in depth and visit all its installations before introducing any operational changes to the company, which Steinbruch says is already well-organized, well-structured and working with competitive prices.

Improvements to the company's sales strategy, however, could bring "very large gains" to CVRD which posted a 1996 profit of $632 million, has total assets of $10.4 billion and annual sales of $5 billion, according to Steinbruch.

"It's not enough to be aggressive on prices. Prices are a consequence of service, quality and proximity to the client," he said. "We have to mobilize on a grand scale to market our product better and adapt it to the needs of particular clients."

This approach could take the form of new joint investments together with CVRD clients or investments directed by clients to create a product suitable to their needs. This is why Steinbruch is traveling to Japan to visit some of CVRD's biggest customers.
Japan, China and Korea represent CVRD's largest export market, accounting for 35 percent of production of 100 million tonnes of iron ore per year, followed by Europe with 25 percent.

He said CVRD's operations in the Amazon mining enclave of Carajas, home to the biggest iron ore deposit in the world of 18 billion tonnes and potentially vast reserves of gold, copper and other metals, should be embraced with particular enthusiasm.
"The area of gold, the area of non-ferrous metals, we plan to push this far more," Steinbruch said.

The company is already Latin America's largest producer of gold with annual output of 18 tonnes and proven reserves of 106.4 tonnes, but its gold fortunes could be considerably higher if a new gold deposit found in 1995 at Serra Leste in the Carajas region proves to hold an estimated 150 tonnes of gold.
CVRD's planned investments totalling $600 million this year are under review, Steinbruch said.
He said the review, which will take three months, could conceivably shift priorities and boost funding.
The new controlling shareholders of CVRD seek to increase productivity by turning each line of business into a separate profit center with its own president.
Under this contemplated restructuring, which still needs to be discussed and approved, CVRD's businesses would be subdivided into ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals, aluminum and pulp and paper.
There are no plans to sell-off any of CVRD's different operations, but Steinbruch did not exclude the possibility once all other options to boost profitability were exhausted.
He said changes in CVRD's organizational structure might add new faces to CVRD's team of executives, but their was no need to replace any of the firm's managers to improve the company's performance.
(--Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
